## Summary

A process post: how Peter's team settled on using LLMs in day-to-day trading research — three pieces plus the payoff.

- **1 — An internal app to explore ideas visually.** "If something catches our attention in a book, a post, an interview or our own trading, we build a view for it." For their current vol-arb research the app studies skew, term structure and how implied volatility behaves around specific events; any U.S. ticker in their database, any day, drill down to a specific minute.
- **2 — The backtester is connected to the app's API.** "When a setup looks interesting on screen, we can test it on exactly the same data." What you eyeballed is what you test — no explorer/backtester data mismatch.
- **3 — The LLM is the scribe around each backtest.** Before a run it helps write down the hypothesis; after the run it automatically summarizes the results and adds screenshots of the setup from the app. "The page shown is one entry in what's become our team's 'second brain.'"
- **The payoff (his words):** "It's easy to get lost in research. This way the book gets written as we go. Months later, someone who didn't run the original backtest can read the results, reopen the same setup in our app and pick up where we left off."

**What the screenshot shows — one entry, "Vol-arb research brain" (OCR read; the near/later numbers were placed by word position, not reading order, and match the constant-maturity tables):**

- **Header — "What it looks like in our app":** "One real trigger: SMH, Thursday 2024-04-04. The screen fired at 15:20. The order filled at 15:25. It is the trigger behind the typical trade of the financed call."
- **Two term-structure panels** (y = 50Δ IV of each listed expiry, x = days to expiry on a log scale; each blue dot is one listed expiry, the orange line is the constant-maturity curve): (1) **a normal day, 2024-03-28** — "near expiry cheaper than the later one - the curve slopes up": near Apr 5 · 8 days · **24.0%** vs later Apr 19 · 22 days · **26.8%**; (2) **the trigger day, 2024-04-04** — "near expiry jumped above the later one - the left end lifted": near Apr 12 · 8 days · **32.1%** vs later May 17 · 43 days · **30.5%**.
- **Constant-maturity table** ("linear in σ²T between the two bracketing expiries; before the front expiry, filled with its IV when it is within about 1.5x the maturity — hollow, italic"). 2026-03-28: 7d 24.0 · 14d 25.7 · 30d 27.7 · 60d 29.0 · 90d 29.8 · 180d 29.9 · 365d 29.8. 2026-04-04: 7d 32.4 · 14d 31.6 · 30d 30.9 · 60d 31.8 · 90d 30.5 · 180d 30.2 · 365d 30.3. On the trigger day the whole front of the curve sat above the back — the mirror image of the normal day.
- **Reopenability in practice — "Where to find it":** their option-analytics app (private LAN address in the screenshot), sidebar Ticker SMH, date panel, Term structure (50Δ IV); "Open the trigger day in the app. Change the date to 2024-03-28 for the left picture."

## Why it matters

- **The LLM is cast as the scribe, not the strategist.** It does the two things researchers skip — writing the hypothesis down *before* the run and the summary *after* — while the human picks the view and the setup. No claim that the LLM finds alpha. The before-run write-up is a pre-registration mechanic: [[2026-10-01-dmartin-hypothesis-first]] states the principle ("no economic mechanism, no build"); Peter's workflow makes it a by-product of running the test at all.
- **"Exactly the same data" closes the explorer/backtester gap** — the chart you saw is the chart you tested, so the note's screenshot and the backtest input cannot silently diverge. And the one-eye-catching-day risk is addressed inside the entry itself: an "Against random entry times" section sits beside "Where it was tested" (presumably the trigger compared with random entries; the content isn't shown).
- **The research log is a by-product, not a chore.** "The book gets written as we go" plus reopenable setups is institutional memory that outlives the person who ran the test — the team-scale version of what this vault does for one reader, and the strongest argument in the vault so far for hypothesis/summary blocks being generated at test time rather than reconstructed later.
- **What the entry template adds to a replication note:** "What can fool it" (failure modes named before the result), "Where it was tested" (sample and benchmark), "What we learned", "Backlinks", "Exits". Cheap to trial on the next replication note — filed as an Inbox task.
- **Skepticism gates:** (1) a process post — zero performance evidence, no backtest numbers, no sample; (2) a hypothesis drafted *after* you have already seen the chart is still post-hoc — the pre-registration value depends on the entry being written before the run and not edited after, and immutability is not mentioned; (3) the auto-summary is written from the same backtest it reports — an LLM summarizer will flatter a result unless the template forces the negative sections ("What can fool it"); (4) one trigger day is shown, the random-entry comparison is only named; (5) it rests on an in-house minute-level options analytics app with a backtester on the same API — not reproducible as-is for a one-person shop; the transferable part is the pattern, not the tooling.
- **Isolation note (CoS convention):** personal second-brain knowledge capture only; nothing routed to the trading company.
